claims.text: The onset of yielding in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide.
Thermal fluctuations enable dislocations to overcome lattice-friction and solute-drag barriers.
Athermal nucleation and FCC-to-BCC phase transformation do not control the onset of yielding.
FeNiCrMn has a large activation volume for dislocation motion, which reduces the strain-rate sensitivity of its flow stress.
High strain rates suppress thermal recovery, causing rapid dislocation accumulation without a proportional increase in yield stress.
The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn material is an annealed, residual-stress-free FCC phase.
The proposed loading program varies temperature from 77 K to 600 K and strain rate from 10^-4 s^-1 to as high as 10^3 s^-1.
Dislocation loops nucleate at surface steps or pre-existing defects.
Dislocations glide on FCC {111} planes in <110> directions.
Lattice distortion and chemical disorder in FeNiCrMn create a high barrier to dislocation motion.
Yield stress follows the stated Arrhenius-type relation sigma = sigma_0 + (kT/V*) ln(epsilon_dot/epsilon_0).
Chemical disorder increases both the effective barrier height and the activation volume in FeNiCrMn.
The FCC phase of FeNiCrMn is stable up to 600 K.
FeNiCrMn has sufficiently high stacking-fault energy to suppress twinning and phase transformation at yield.
Yield strength will have a strain-rate slope of approximately 10–20 MPa per decade.
Yield strength will be approximately 800 MPa at 77 K and 400 MPa at 600 K.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur at the onset of yielding.
Traditional FCC metals such as Ni and Cu exhibit strain-rate sensitivities of approximately 30–50 MPa per decade.
Crystal orientation significantly affects the critical resolved shear stress and onset of plasticity.
Detection of BCC diffraction peaks at yield is proposed as a falsifying outcome for the no-transformation hypothesis.
